**Video:** [Tutorial 14 Part 1 — CNNs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0wd-LIzzfM0)

## Learning goals

- See a CNN as an MLP with **local receptive fields** and **weight sharing**.
- Compute a tiny 1-D / 2-D convolution and a pooling step by hand.
- Name the usual stack: conv $\to$ nonlinearity $\to$ pool $\to$ (repeat) $\to$ dense head.

## Before this clicks

An image is a grid of numbers (channels $\times$ height $\times$ width). A fully connected layer on flattened pixels has one weight per pixel–unit pair — huge, and it ignores that nearby pixels matter more. A **filter** (kernel) is a small weight patch slid across the grid; the same weights are reused everywhere (**parameter sharing**). That is the practical heart of a CNN.

---

## Main ideas

### 1. Convolution as a local weighted sum

For a 1-D signal $x$ and filter $w$ of length $k$, a valid convolution output at position $t$ is

$$
z_t=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1} w_j\, x_{t+j}
$$

(plus a bias $b$ in practice). In 2-D, sum over a $k\times k$ window (and over input channels). Sliding the window builds a **feature map**.

### 2. Why this helps on images

| Idea | Plain English |
|------|----------------|
| Local connectivity | Each unit sees a patch, not the whole image |
| Weight sharing | One edge detector is reused at every location |
| Translation equivariance | Shift the input $\Rightarrow$ feature map shifts similarly |

Fewer parameters than a dense MLP of similar “coverage,” and the inductive bias matches natural images.

### 3. Nonlinearity and pooling

After conv, apply an elementwise activation (commonly ReLU: $\max(0,z)$). **Pooling** (e.g. max over $2\times 2$) downsamples: keeps a strong local response, shrinks spatial size, adds mild translation robustness.

### 4. Stacking and the classifier head

Early layers tend to pick edges/textures; deeper maps become more abstract. Flatten (or global-pool) the last maps and feed a small MLP for class scores. Training uses the same backprop story as MLPs; gradients flow through the shared filters.

### 5. Practical batching intuition

A minibatch is a 4-D tensor: `(batch, channels, height, width)`. One forward pass applies the same filters to every sample in the batch. Data augmentation (crops, flips) is common because CNNs still overfit when labels are scarce.

---

## Worked mini-example

Input row $x=[1,2,0,3]$, filter $w=[1,-1]$, bias $0$, valid conv:

$$
z_0=1\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 2=-1,\quad
z_1=1\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0=2,\quad
z_2=1\cdot 0+(-1)\cdot 3=-3.
$$

ReLU $\Rightarrow$ $[0,2,0]$. Max-pool with width $2$, stride $2$ on $[0,2,0]$ (pad or drop the last) $\Rightarrow$ e.g. $\max(0,2)=2$. Same arithmetic, in 2-D, is what a first CNN layer does on a tiny patch.

---

## Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Convolution “understands” objects by itself | Filters learn from data; architecture only biases locality/sharing |
| Pooling is required | Common, not sacred; stride-in-conv can downsample instead |
| More filters always better | Capacity $\uparrow$ and overfit risk $\uparrow$; need data/regularization |
| CNN $\neq$ MLP | It **is** a constrained MLP; the constraints are the point |

3. Why share one filter across locations?
